description: AI Engineer in Ottawa with a Master’s in CS (AI & ML) from the University of York and a Graduate Certificate in AI Software Development from Algonquin College. I’ve spent years building ML, computer vision and NLP solutions as a freelancer, mostly in Python, and published research on spam filtering and lung cancer diagnosis. Excited to work with NASA’s open data and help with modeling, data pipelines or design. Looking for a collaborative team to build something impactful.
summary: AURA (Autonomous Unified Risk Assessment) helps astronauts on long missions assess their own health when the flight surgeon is minutes away. From Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way, so the crew must be its own first line of care. Health changes are often gradual and look normal by Earth standards while already abnormal for that person. AURA compares every reading with the astronaut's own preflight baseline and gives a clear Normal, Warning or Critical status with the reason. It forecasts trends 14 days ahead, turns alerts into a daily plan, triages symptoms, tracks radiation against NASA's career limit, and sends messages to the ground with the real signal delay, answered live from a flight surgeon console. Crew can ask AURA questions by voice, transcribed on board. Transparent, cited rules set every alert; Claude AI only explains and coaches, with an offline fallback. AURA runs on real NASA OSDR data from the Inspiration4 crew, alongside clearly labelled synthetic telemetry. Longer missions need crews who can spot trouble early and act on it, and the same approach can help isolated teams on Earth, such as Antarctic stations.
details:
The problem. On Moon and Mars missions, astronauts face NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. A message to the flight surgeon takes 1.3 seconds from the Moon but up to about 12.5 minutes each way from Mars. Most health changes are gradual and stay inside normal Earth ranges while already being abnormal for that person, so a one-size-fits-all threshold misses them.

The motivation. As an AI engineer and computer science graduate, I (Ibrahim) have long been fascinated by AI-driven healthcare, and curious about how artificial intelligence can support medical care. This challenge puts that question in its hardest setting: a crew that has to look after itself when the doctor is minutes away. It pushed us to build AI that helps people understand their own health, while every alert stays transparent, rule-based and safe.


What AURA does.

  • Personal baselines. Seven preflight days set each astronaut's own normal for 10 indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise, radiation). Every indicator maps to one of NASA's five hazards and cites its source.
  • Clear status with the reason. Transparent rules give Normal, Warning or Critical, flagging limits, sustained shifts and unusual readings, with a body map and plain-language next steps.
  • Early warning. Trends are projected 14 days ahead with a 95% range. In the demo, AURA flags the flight engineer's rising heart rate days before it becomes a warning.
  • From alert to action. A daily plan adjusts exercise, sleep, light and social time to today's alerts and says why. Symptom triage uses fixed rules, and red flags always mean contacting the ground.
  • Radiation budget. Career and 30-day dose are tracked against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, including dose from earlier missions.
  • Distance from Earth. Message ground drafts an urgent message with the status attached and shows the real signal delay for the ISS, a lunar base or a Mars transit. A delivery status shows each message as Sent, Delivered to Earth, Seen and Replied. A ground view sorts the whole crew by priority and prints reports, and a Flight surgeon console lets a real person answer from a second device, with the same delay both ways.
  • Crew wellbeing. A team wellbeing score, a gamified routine with streaks, badges and weekly challenges, and a crew board keep measuring a habit on long missions.
  • AI that explains, never decides. Claude writes a daily briefing, answers typed or spoken questions through Ask AURA (which reads answers aloud and takes you to any page you ask for), and reviews real astronaut bloodwork. Rules always set the level, and a critical reading always escalates.
  • Real NASA data. Inspiration4 crew bloodwork, 80 immune and cardiac cytokines and proteins, and 200-plex serum and urine panels from NASA OSDR, from 92 days before launch to 194 days after return. One finding: IL-6, an inflammation signal, was higher the day after landing than 3 days before launch in all four crew members.
  • Your own data. Edit the crew, import a CSV from a wearable or lab, or add your own indicators.

How it works. A Python FastAPI back end holds the rule engine, forecast, planner and data parsers. A React front end shows a landing page and 12 feature pages. Claude is called through the Anthropic API, with a rule-based fallback for every AI feature, so AURA works offline, which matters with Mars delays. 193 automated tests cover the rules and data. Data quality checks drop a misaligned published row and readings stuck at an assay's measurement limit.

Benefits. Astronauts catch problems earlier, know exactly what to do, and know when to call the ground. Flight surgeons see who needs attention first. Every alert is explainable and traceable to a cited rule.

What we hope to achieve. A self-assessment tool that stays useful when Earth is minutes away, and the same approach for isolated crews on Earth, such as Antarctic stations and analog missions.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, pytest, React, Vite, Recharts, the Anthropic Claude API, Whisper (faster-whisper) for on-device speech recognition, Docker, Render and Vercel.
